intro: The finale of Mozart’s Symphony No. 40 in G minor, K. 550, marked Allegro assai, opens with a rising string arpeggio played piano, and the full orchestra replies forte. The lyrical second theme later returns in G minor, and the movement stays in that key to the end.

sections.label: A · Rising string arpeggio, full orchestra replies
sections.mNote: A quiet arpeggio climbs through G minor.

sections.label: B · Second theme in B♭ major
sections.mNote: Violins and winds share the second theme.

sections.label: Dev · Arpeggio theme fragmented
sections.mNote: Chromatic unison, then fragments in imitation.

sections.label: A′ · G minor leaping theme returns
sections.mNote: The quiet string phrase and its forceful continuation return.

sections.label: B′ · Second theme in G minor
sections.mNote: The second theme returns in the tonic, G minor.

cues.title: Opening theme, bars 1–16
cues.text: The strings rise through a G minor chord. The orchestra follows with a forceful rushing figure. Mozart alternates the spare rising phrase with the fuller, crowded reply throughout the opening.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 1–16. The triadic opening and rushing violin response are described by Marianne Williams Tobias: https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second theme in B♭ major
cues.text: The second theme is in B♭ major, shared between violins and winds. It moves in longer note values than the material around it. The accompanying pulse continues underneath.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, second group, pp. 37–38 of the numbered scan; Tobias’s Indianapolis Symphony note describes the violin-and-wind melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Charles Rosen on Mozart’s suffering
cues.text: The pianist and critic Charles Rosen wrote: “In all of Mozart’s supreme expressions of suffering and terror … there is something shockingly voluptuous.”
cues.evidence: Charles Rosen, as quoted in Michael Steinberg, The Symphony: A Listener’s Guide (Oxford, 1995), and in Marianne Williams Tobias’s Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra programme note: https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/. In the original sentence the dash list continues through the G minor Symphony, Don Giovanni and Pamina’s aria; Rosen’s own book was not opened.

cues.title: Opening of the development
cues.text: At the development, the opening leap returns in unison, with chromatic notes added. The strings then pass fragments of it between them in overlapping entries.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 125–170: chromatic opening of the development and subsequent imitative writing.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Orchestra without trumpets or timpani
cues.text: The whole symphony is scored for horns, woodwinds and strings. Mozart left out trumpets and timpani, and the finale’s loudest passages are played by this comparatively small orchestra.
cues.evidence: Instrumentation in both versions of K. 550, listed at https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.40_in_G_minor,_K.550_(Mozart,_Wolfgang_Amadeus).

cues.title: Recapitulation, bar 206
cues.text: The rising figure returns piano in G minor, followed as before by its loud reply. After the chromatic passages of the development, it again outlines the notes of the tonic chord.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, recapitulation from bar 206.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second theme in G minor
cues.text: The second theme, first heard in B♭ major, returns in G minor in the recapitulation. The movement stays in G minor to the final chords.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, recapitulated second group and final cadence, pp. 46–49 of the numbered scan.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Critical reception of K. 550
cues.text: Neal Zaslaw wrote of K. 550: “No symphony of Mozart’s, not even the ‘Jupiter’, has aroused so much comment as this one.” In the nineteenth century Otto Jahn heard in it “sorrow and complaining”, and in the finale “a wild merriment that seeks to drown sorrow”.
cues.evidence: Neal Zaslaw, Mozart’s Symphonies: Context, Performance Practice, Reception (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1989): the sentence appears in the book (Internet Archive full-text excerpt, page not seen) and is quoted in Marianne Williams Tobias’s note: https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/. Otto Jahn, Life of Mozart, trans. P. D. Townsend (1882), vol. 3, chapter on instrumental music: “Sorrow and complaining take the place of joy and gladness”; the finale “brings no peace, only a wild merriment that seeks to drown sorrow”: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/43413

transitions.title: Dominant of B♭ before the second theme
transitions.from: A · Rising string arpeggio, full orchestra replies
transitions.to: B · Second theme in B♭ major
transitions.how: The transition comes to rest on F, the dominant of B♭ major. After the break, violins and woodwinds share the quieter second theme. It moves in longer notes than the rushing answer of the opening, and the Allegro assai tempo continues.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, transition and second-group opening, pp. 36–37 of the numbered scan.

transitions.title: From exposition to development
transitions.from: B · Second theme in B♭ major
transitions.how: The exposition closes in B♭ major. The development opens with the opening leap stretched into a chromatic line played in unison by the orchestra, with no supporting chord. The strings then take up fragments of it in imitation, each entry following the one before.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 118–140.

transitions.title: Return from D to G minor
transitions.to: A′ · G minor leaping theme returns
transitions.how: Running fragments in the strings move to D, the dominant of G minor (bars 193–214). The opening arpeggio then returns quietly in the strings, over the same G minor harmony as at the start of the movement. The loud reply follows, as it does in the opening bars.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 193–214.

transitions.title: Dominant preparation for the second theme
transitions.from: A′ · G minor leaping theme returns
transitions.to: B′ · Second theme in G minor
transitions.how: In the recapitulation the transition prepares G minor through its dominant, D. Violins and winds then resume the quieter second theme in the home key. Where the exposition moved to B♭ major for this theme, the melody now returns in G minor, and the orchestral contrast between the groups is kept.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, recapitulatory transition and second group, pp. 45–47 of the numbered scan.

source.title: Mozart, Symphony No. 40, K. 550, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke VIII/40 (1880), plate W.A.M. 550; parts common to both versions
source.locator: IV. Allegro assai, PDF pp. 33–49: opening arpeggio, second theme, development and recapitulation. The edition prints both orchestral versions.

timeline.note: The violins’ quiet rising arpeggio is supported by bassoons and lower strings.
Winds and horns reinforce the running string figures.
The violins’ B♭ major tune alternates with replies from the wind.
The opening arpeggio breaks into a chromatic unison, then passes between imitating parts.
The quiet rising arpeggio returns in the violins, with bassoons and lower strings.
The second theme returns in G minor, with strings and winds answering each other.
The strings play running figures up to the close beneath held and accented wind chords.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to play the finale through. The work was K. 466 in D minor. It opens with syncopated strings, and the piano enters with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert excellent.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart later dedicated the quartets to him.
